catalog_quote: Stress has a low functional load in Lio and is usually initial in isolated words. This applies also words with schwa in the first syllable, but these words then receive a geminated medial consonant. watu [ˈwatʰu] ‘stone’, lako [ˈlakʰo] ‘dog’, ebé [ˈʔəbːe] ‘they; 3pl’. The main class of exceptions to this are words with medial /r/. Medial /r/ does not become geminated when it follows schwa, but instead remains as it is, and the stress shifts rightward to the final syllable. peri [pəˈri] ‘bamboo species’, mera [məˈra] ‘to live’. The usual rule of stress assignment to the first syllable of each word, in conjunction with the tendency of Lio words to contain two syllables, leads to a very common phrasal pattern of initial stress, followed by alternating unstressed and stressed syllables. ... new_statements.quote: Stress has a low functional load in Lio and is usually initial in isolated words. This applies also words with schwa in the first syllable, but these words then receive a geminated medial consonant. watu [ˈwatʰu] 'stone', lako [ˈlakʰo] 'dog', ebé [ˈʔəbːe] 'they; 3pl'. The main class of exceptions to this are words with medial /r/. Medial /r/ does not become geminated when it follows schwa, but instead remains as it is, and the stress shifts rightward to the final syllable. peri [pəˈri] 'bamboo species', mera [məˈra] 'to live'. The usual rule of stress assignment to the first syllable of each word, in conjunction with the tendency of Lio words to contain two syllables, leads to a very common phrasal pattern of initial stress, followed by alternating unstressed and stressed syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllable of the (maximally disyllabic, bimoraic) native word, i.e. initial = penultimate in disyllables; monosyllables are lengthened and stressed. Stress is non-contrastive (low functional load).
new_statements.secondary_stress: No word-internal secondary stress (native words have at most two syllables); at phrase level the initial-stress rule yields an alternating stressed-unstressed pattern; class terms and reduced function words 'often bear a weak secondary stress or no stress at all' and cliticize to a neighbouring word (p. 64).
new_statements.exceptions: Words with schwa in the first syllable and medial /r/ take final stress (peri [pəˈri], mera [məˈra], seré [səˈre]); more generally stress on schwa-initial words is 'somewhat unpredictable' (some final, some initial, some varying with prosodic context, Sec. 2.4.2 p. 50); unstressed function words (clitics) bear no stress; author notes the rules 'do not account for the placement of stress in all Lio phrases'. Nothing said about stress in longer loanwords.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is for isolated words (citation forms); phrasal rhythm described separately (ex. 12-14). Variety described: Lio of Detukeli (Western Lio), fieldwork 2017.
new_statements.identity_note: Elias 2018 describes Lio as spoken in Detukeli (Western Lio dialect, Kab. Ende), glottocode lioo1240 (no separate dialect code known); Wivell 2022's second-hand restatement concerns the self-identified 'Lio Aku' dialect of Wolondopo. Both are Li'o [ljl].
